summary: Specifies security mechanisms for the IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Protocol (NDP), which is vulnerable to attacks if unsecured. Unlike the original specifications, SEND does not use IPsec.

plainLanguage.summary: When two computers on the same network ask each other for a phone number (a link-layer address), SEND adds a signature and a proof of identity. That means an attacker on the link cannot easily pretend to be someone else or to be the network's router.

subtitle: How to secure IPv6 Neighbor Discovery on a link without needing manual IPsec security associations.

tldr.problem: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery (NDP) lets any node on a link claim an address or pose as a router; the original plan to use IPsec required manual security associations that were impractical for most links.
tldr.mechanism: SEND adds new ND options: Cryptographically Generated Addresses (CGA) prove address ownership, an RSA Signature option signs the message, Timestamp and Nonce options prevent replay, and an Authorization Delegation Discovery process lets hosts verify routers via certification paths to a trust anchor.
tldr.outcome: Hosts can tell genuine routers from impersonators and reject spoofed ND messages, while secured and unsecured ND can coexist. RFC 3971 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 6494, RFC 6495 and RFC 6980.

facts.label: ND option types
facts.value: 11 CGA, 12 RSA Signature, 13 Timestamp, 14 Nonce, 15 Trust Anchor, 16 Certificate

facts.label: RSA signature
facts.value: RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 with SHA-1 over SEND-signed data

facts.label: Nonce length
facts.value: ≥ 6 bytes, padded to multiple of 8 octets

facts.label: Authorization model
facts.value: X.509 certification paths with optional prefix constraints; null prefix ::/0 or no extension means unconstrained

today: RFC 3971 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2005. It has been updated by RFC 6494, RFC 6495 and RFC 6980, and no RFC obsoletes it. Read those updates alongside this text when implementing.

sections.title: What This RFC Does
sections.content:
IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Protocol (NDP) runs on a link and handles Address Resolution, Neighbor Unreachability Detection (NUD), Duplicate Address Detection (DAD), Router Discovery (RD) and Redirection. The original NDP specs suggested IPsec, but doing so needs manual security associations and scales poorly. RFC 3971 defines SEcure Neighbor Discovery (SEND), which secures NDP using public-key signatures and CGAs instead of requiring manually keyed IPsec SAs.

SEND is for environments where link physical security is not assured (such as wireless) and NDP attacks are a concern. It supports coexistence of secured and unsecured NDP. Proxy ND and using identity certificates on end hosts to authorize address use are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC explains how to lock the local phone-book that computers use to find each other, without the tangle of pre-shared keys.

sections.title: How SEND Works in Broad Terms
sections.content:
SEND adds new NDP options and a small authorization discovery process:

  • CGA option: proves the sender owns the claimed address via a Cryptographically Generated Address.
  • RSA Signature option: signs the NDP message so receivers can verify it came from the key tied to that address or to an authorized router.
  • Timestamp and Nonce options: prevent replay attacks (Timestamp protects unsolicited/multicast messages, Nonce protects solicitation–advertisement pairs).
  • Authorization Delegation Discovery (ADD): lets hosts get a certification path from a router to a trust anchor via Certification Path Solicitation (CPS, ICMPv6 Type 148) and Certification Path Advertisement (CPA, ICMPv6 Type 149), so hosts can verify routers are authorized to advertise prefixes.

Router authorization is based on X.509 certificates (per [RFC3280]) with an optional X.509 IP address extension listing the prefixes a router may advertise; if unconstrained (null prefix or no extension) the router may advertise any prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: Each secure message carries: proof the address is not stolen (CGA), a signature, a timestamp or a one-time number to stop reuse, and certificates that prove the router is allowed to speak for the network.

sections.title: The New Neighbor Discovery Options
sections.content:
Six new options are defined. CGA option (Type 11) carries the CGA Parameters structure ([RFC3972]); if both CGA and RSA Signature are present, the public key in CGA Parameters is the one used by the signature. RSA Signature option (Type 12) carries a 128-bit Key Hash (SHA-1 of the public key used in CGA or the certified key) and a PKCS#1 v1.5 signature over a specific byte sequence that includes a 128-bit SEND CGA Message Type tag (0x086F CA5E ...), the IP source and destination, ICMPv6 type/code/checksum, the NDP message header up to options, and all options preceding the RSA Signature option. Timestamp option (Type 13) is a 64-bit fixed-point seconds since 1970-01-01 00:00 UTC (48-bit seconds, 16-bit fractional 1/2^16 s). Nonce option (Type 14) carries at least 6 bytes of random data chosen by the solicitor and echoed by the responder. Trust Anchor option (Type 15) names a trust anchor (Name Type 1 = DER-encoded X.501 name; Name Type 2 = FQDN). Certificate option (Type 16) carries an X.509v3 certificate.

SEND requires RSA for signatures (single algorithm to avoid interoperability complexity); a stronger algorithm can be introduced later as a revision.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol adds six small stamps to messages: one proves the address, one proves the signer wrote it, one dates it, one ties it to a question, one names who to trust, and one carries the certificate.

sections.title: When Options Must Appear
sections.content:
Nodes configured to use SEND MUST include the CGA option in NS and NA, and in RS unless RS is sent from the unspecified address. The RSA Signature option MUST be present in NS, NA, RA and Redirect; it MUST be present in RS when not sent from the unspecified address. All SEND messages MUST include a Timestamp; solicitations MUST include a Nonce and responders MUST include the same Nonce in the solicited advertisement.

Receivers discard messages missing required options (treating as unsecured only in the mixed/coexistence policy defined in Section 8). RSA Signature is the last option. A received message's Key Hash must match a known public key (from CGA in the same message or known otherwise). If a trust anchor is configured, a valid certification path from that trust anchor to the sender's key must be known for router messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Every secure question and answer carries a date-stamp and a one-time code. Routers must also prove they are trusted, hosts must prove they own their address.

sections.title: Addresses and Prefix Authorization
sections.content:
SEND uses Cryptographically Generated Addresses so that ownership of an address can be verified from the public key in the CGA Parameters. The specification also allows non-CGAs with certificates authorizing their use, but that is out of scope. Redirect addresses must not be forged in a way that breaks this model. A router may advertise a set of prefixes; a host checks that each advertised prefix falls within the ranges authorized by the router's certification path. If the certificate has the null prefix (::/0) or no prefix extension, the router is unconstrained (may advertise any prefix). Certified prefixes may be constrained per router or per delegation.

Hosts doing stateless autoconfiguration SHOULD use a certified prefix; if none match, they SHOULD try a different advertising router. For stateful autoconfiguration, the offered address's prefix SHOULD be checked against certified prefixes.
sections.plainLanguage: An address can be made to carry its own proof (a CGA). A router cannot lie about which network prefixes it is allowed to serve; the certificates limit it.

sections.title: Secured and Unsecured Can Coexist
sections.content: On a mixed link, secured messages (those with a valid RSA Signature) take priority. SEND nodes may be configured to ignore all unsecured NS/NA/RS/RA/Redirect messages (to enforce SEND-only), but the default is to allow both. A SEND node MUST send secured messages for its own solicitations and unsolicited advertisements, and MUST respond to a secured solicitation with a secured advertisement. When DAD is run, unsecured responses are accepted only for the first tentative CGA attempt (to avoid breaking attach on legacy links); for subsequent attempts unsecured responses are ignored. Neighbor Cache, Prefix List and Default Router List entries are marked secured or unsecured; unsecured messages must not change secured entries. A node MAY adopt an unsecured router or one still undergoing security checks while verifying, but SHOULD prefer a secured router once fully verified.
sections.plainLanguage: New secure machines and old insecure machines can share the same wire. Secure machines trust only what is properly signed, unless told otherwise, but by default they do not refuse to speak at all.

sections.title: Security Considerations in Brief
sections.content: SEND counters spoofing of NS/NA (address ownership via CGA + signature), protects NUD from false reachability claims, raises the cost of DAD DoS, and secures RS/RA against router impersonation by requiring router authorization via certification paths and signatures. Timestamp and Nonce defend against replay. Rate limiting on CPS/CPA helps mitigate DoS from authorization discovery. Known limitations: SEND does not provide confidentiality; it does not fix a completely unsecured link layer (e.g. MAC spoofing is still possible at layer 2); MLD is not secured; static addresses and non-CGA fixed IID cases are not covered by this base spec; and proxy ND is out of scope. Trust anchor provisioning is deployment-dependent (centralized or decentralized).
sections.plainLanguage: SEND stops most local impersonation and replay tricks, but it cannot hide traffic and it cannot stop someone who can fully fake the underlying wire. It also needs someone to decide who counts as a legitimate router.

left.title: Timestamp option (Type 13)
left.desc: Used to prevent replay of unsolicited or multicast messages; checked against a recent window (with fuzz and allowed drift).

right.title: Nonce option (Type 14)
right.desc: Random value chosen by the solicitor in RS/NS and echoed by the responder in RA/NA; prevents replay of solicited advertisements.

fields.name: Key Hash
fields.desc: Leftmost 128 bits of SHA-1 of the public key

fields.name: Digital Signature
fields.desc: PKCS#1 v1.5 RSA-SHA1 signature (variable; shown as block)

messages.label: Certification Path Solicitation (ICMPv6 Type 148)
messages.note: Host asks for certification path to one of its configured trust anchors; includes Trust Anchor option(s).

messages.label: Certification Path Advertisement (ICMPv6 Type 149)
messages.note: Router returns the certification path components (as Certificate options) so the host can validate against its trust anchor.

messages.label: Secured RS/RA verified against trust anchor and CGA+signature
messages.note: Now host can safely accept RA prefixes and use the router as default (subject to timestamp/nonce checks).
